Read the text and answer.
The sense of smell is closely linked to memory, which explains why a familiar scent can instantly recall an event from childhood. Researchers believe that this connection exists because the part of the brain that processes smell lies next to the regions responsible for emotion and memory. Unlike other senses, smell signals do not pass through the thalamus, the brain's main relay station, before reaching these areas. As a result, scent-triggered memories are often more emotional than memories evoked by sight or sound. Perfume makers and supermarkets have long exploited this effect; some stores release the aroma of fresh bread near the entrance to encourage shoppers to buy more. In recent years, scientists have also begun to test scent therapy for patients with early dementia, although results so far remain inconclusive and larger trials, involving at least 500 participants, are planned.

Why can a scent recall memories so quickly?
Smell is the strongest of all senses.
The area that processes smell lies next to the areas for emotion and memory.
